newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: UN official dubs Colombia "feudal nation".
newsitem.headline: UN official dubs Colombia "feudal nation".

text.p: A U.N. official said in a newspaper interview on Sunday that Colombia was becoming a "feudal nation" where everybody sets up their own "private army."

The comments made in the face of escalating political violence across the country are unlikely to endear Almudena Mazarrasa, the U.N. high commissioner for human rights in this Andean nation, to the Colombian authorities, who already accuse her of being soft the leftist guerrillas.

"The rise in violence is terrifying. I'm shocked to be witnessing all these atrocities," Mazarrasa, who is from Spain, told the El Tiempo newspaper. "Colombia seems like it is becoming a country where anybody that pleases sets up their own private army."

Mazarrasa has already offended some sectors of the Colombian government, some of the military top brass and Alvaro Uribe, the hardline governor of northwest Antioquia province, for her outspoken criticism of legal civilian self-defense groups known as "Convivir."

The U.N. official said earlier this month that the Convivirs, whose stated role is to provide intelligence data on guerrilla movements to the armed forces, were committing rights abuses against suspected rebel sympathizers. International human rights groups have criticized the Convivirs for being little more than legalized vigilante groups, often connected to right-wing death squads.

"The U.N. has never opposed citizens' rights to self-defense but the law (on Convivirs) gives these groups the possibility to obtain military-issue weapons which is worrying in the light of international humanitarian law," Mazarrasa told El Tiempo.

Contrary to official allegations, the U.N. commissioner, who opened her office in Bogota earlier this year, also had harsh words for the country's leftist guerrillas, criticizing their widespread tactics of extortion and kidnapping as a means of filling their war chests.

Mazarrasa also questioned the rebels' will for peace and said they should not ignore President Ernesto Samper's calls to launch a new peace process to end Colombia's three-decade-old internal conflict.
"The guerrillas' refusal to sit down at the negotiating table is lamentable and worrying...they're not just ignoring the wishes of a government but of all society," she said.
